questions.stem: What does the Halting Problem ask?

options.text: Whether a program will halt on a given input.
Whether a program is syntactically correct.
Whether a program will execute efficiently.
Whether a program will produce the correct output.

questions.explanation: The Halting Problem specifically asks if there is an algorithm to determine whether any given program will stop running or continue indefinitely on a particular input.

distractorRationale.b: Syntactic correctness is checked by compilers, not related to the Halting Problem.
distractorRationale.c: Efficiency is a performance concern, not a decidability issue.
distractorRationale.d: Correct output is about correctness, not halting.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the diagonalization argument?

options.text: A method to find a contradiction by assuming a solution exists.
A technique for optimizing algorithms.
A process to check program syntax.
A way to measure program efficiency.

questions.explanation: The diagonalization argument is used to demonstrate that assuming a solution to the Halting Problem leads to a logical contradiction, proving that no such solution can exist.

distractorRationale.c: It does not relate to syntax checking.
distractorRationale.d: It is unrelated to efficiency measurement.

questions.stem: Why is the Halting Problem undecidable?

options.text: Because it leads to a logical contradiction if assumed decidable.
Because it is too complex for modern computers.
Because there are too many programs to check.
Because it requires infinite memory to solve.

questions.explanation: The Halting Problem is undecidable because assuming a solution exists leads to a contradiction, as shown by the diagonalization argument.

distractorRationale.b: Complexity is not the reason for undecidability.
distractorRationale.c: The number of programs is not the core issue.
distractorRationale.d: Memory requirements are not the reason for undecidability.
